idiom_name: { it } / ::identity — lambda-literal pass-through; no stdlib identity function
implementation_notes: Kotlin's standard library ships no identity function (unlike Scala's Predef.identity or Java's Function.identity()), so the classic structure collapses into the language's own function-type machinery: wherever a (T) -> T slot exists, the lambda literal { it } — with the implicit single-parameter name it — is the canonical pass-through, as in nested.flatMap { it } or names.map { it }. The reusable polymorphic form is a generic single-expression function fun <T> identity(x: T): T = x, passed as ::identity, because a generic val property is illegal in Kotlin and therefore no one-size identity value can be imported. Since the usual consumers are inline higher-order functions (map/filter/fold/let/also), the pass-through body is copied into the call site and costs neither a Function1 allocation nor a virtual invoke(); only piping { it } through a non-inline function-type boundary pays that overhead. The named-function form is still justified when the identity is stored in collections, passed across module boundaries, or referenced repeatedly, where one shared ::identity reads better than scattered { it } literals.
pitfalls: Kotlin has no stdlib identity and generic val properties are illegal, so teams hand-roll per-type copies like val identity = { x: X -> x } that drift apart; declare one generic fun <T> identity(x: T): T = x (or plain { it }) instead of duplicating the concept per file.

Every function value is an object: piped through a non-inline function-type boundary, { it } allocates a Function1 and pays a virtual invoke() per call; keep pass-through steps inside inline higher-order functions (map/filter/fold/let) or hoist one shared reference in hot paths.

{ it } only fits single-parameter function types: a fold's (acc: R, T) -> R combiner needs { _, x -> x }; Kotlin's type system rejects wrong-arity stand-ins at compile time, so fix the shape rather than weakening a parameter to Any?.

sortedBy { it } and sortBy { it } are legal no-op sort keys that hide a forgotten key derivation where natural-order sorted() was meant; likewise x.let { it } reads like a transformation yet does nothing — delete or tag these in review.

Identity propagates exceptions unchanged: substituting it for a missing error-handling strategy in a pipeline chain does not make the chain safe — failures still surface at the next non-pass-through stage.
